newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan leader refuses to knuckle under in hog row.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan leader refuses to knuckle under in hog row.

text.p: Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui on Wednesday joined a drive to ease public fears over the island's devastating hog epidemic, eating pig knuckles at a televised "eat-in" to restore confidence in pork.

Sporting a vest reading "Eating pork is healthy and safe", Lee made his personal bid to soften the blow of a foot-and-mouth disease outbreak, announced on March 20, that has forced a pork export ban, the slaughter of two million pigs and a tumble in pork prices.
"We can eat it ourselves (and) export it," Lee told reporters.
"Let's take it slowly," he added, accompanied at the Taipei "eat-in" by the ruling Nationalist Party's leadership.
Vice-President Lien Chan raised a toast. "Eat with good health, with prosperity," Lien said between bites.
Gnawing on pig knuckles in public was a bold gesture to counter weeks of graphic television coverage of the effect of the disease -- festering, infected hog hooves.

Consumers have turned away in droves from what in normal times was their staple meat, sending pork prices plummeting 60 percent since the crisis hit and rocking Taiwan's feed importers and meatpackers.
Analysts have said the epidemic could shave as much as one percentage point off Taiwan's gross domestic product growth in 1997, a major setback to its hard-won economic recovery.
Lee called for a review of the all-out pork export ban which was imposed on March 20, suggesting it might have been an over-reaction.
"We have the world's best hog breeding skill," said Lee, who holds a Cornell University doctorate in agricultural economics.
"We should consult farm experts' advice on pork exports and not change our polices simply because of one incident like foot-and-mouth disease," he said.
Though a lifting of the ban was not imminent, officials said they were exploring 13 new overseas pork markets in a bid to cope with the epidemic that has wiped out Taiwan's huge exports to Japan.
They include Vietnam, Malaysia, Italy and Britain. Japan and Korea have banned imports of Taiwan pork. The Philippines has gone further, excluding meat from any Taiwan livestock.
"We must make sure our pork is 100 percent safe for export and then ease the ban before others will consider it," said Liao An-ting of the cabinet's Council of Agriculture.
The council last month banned exports and ordered a mass slaughter and inoculation drive after confirming an outbreak of the deadly contagious foot-and-mouth disease at nine hog farms.
The airborne virus has spread to 2,469 of Taiwan's 25,000 hog farms, with officials projecting that 2.16 million of the island's 14 million pigs would have to be destroyed.
Farmers and soldiers were slaughtering all hogs -- healthy or otherwise -- at all affected farms, while all cloven-hoofed livestock were being vaccinated at healthy farms.
President Lee also called for a crackdown on pork smuggling from mainland China, which experts have identified as the most likely origin of the foot-and-mouth virus.
